questions.question_text:
An earthquake has amplitude $A=10^{8}$.
Using $M=\log_{10}A$, what is its Richter magnitude?

options.why: Multiplied the amplitude by ten instead of taking its logarithm.
Miscounted the power of ten, using one less than the index.
Gave the amplitude $10^{8}$ as a number instead of its magnitude.

questions.question_text:
An earthquake has Richter magnitude $M=7$.
Using $A=10^{M}$, what is the amplitude $A$?

options.why: Multiplied the magnitude by ten instead of raising ten to the magnitude.
Used one less in the index, computing $10^{6}$.
Raised the wrong base, computing $2^{7}$ instead of $10^{7}$.

questions.question_text:
One earthquake measures magnitude $6$ and another measures magnitude $2$ on the Richter scale.
How many times greater is the amplitude of the larger earthquake?

options.why: Used the difference in magnitude directly instead of $10^{4}$.
Raised ten to the larger magnitude instead of the difference.
Divided the magnitudes rather than subtracting them.
Used the difference of $2$ magnitudes instead of $10^{2}$.
Treated the two-step gap as a single times-ten step.
Used a difference of three magnitudes instead of two.

questions.solution_text:
From the graph, Tonga has magnitude $6$ and Alaska has magnitude $4$.
$\dfrac{A_{1}}{A_{2}}=\dfrac{10^{6}}{10^{4}}$
$=10^{2}$
$=100$
So the amplitude was $100$ times greater.

questions.question_text:
A solution has hydrogen-ion concentration $M=10^{-6}$ mol/L.
Using $pH=-\log_{10}M$, what is its pH?

options.why: Forgot the minus sign in $pH=-\log_{10}M$.
Miscounted the concentration as $10^{-5}$.
Gave the concentration $10^{-6}$ instead of the pH value.

questions.question_text:
How many times more intense is a $90$ dB sound than a $40$ dB sound?
Use $\dfrac{I}{I_{0}}=10^{S/10}$.

options.why: Used the decibel difference of $50$ directly as the answer.
Stopped at the index $5$ instead of evaluating $10^{5}$.
Used a difference of $30$ dB instead of $50$ dB.

questions.question_text:
On a base-$10$ logarithmic scale, quantity P has magnitude $7$ and quantity Q has magnitude $3$.
How many times larger is P than Q?

options.why: Used the difference of $4$ magnitudes instead of $10^{4}$.
Raised ten to P's magnitude instead of the difference.
Multiplied the two magnitudes together.

questions.solution_text:
The magnitudes differ by $7-3=4$.
So P is $10^{4}=10\,000$ times larger than Q.

questions.question_text:
Solution P has $pH=2$ and solution Q has $pH=5$.
Using $M=10^{-pH}$, how many times greater is the hydrogen-ion concentration in solution P?

options.why: Used the pH difference of $3$ directly instead of $10^{3}$.
Reversed the ratio, missing that a lower pH means a higher concentration.
Used a difference of two instead of three in the index.

questions.solution_text:
$M=10^{-pH}$
For P: $M=10^{-2}$.
For Q: $M=10^{-5}$.
$\dfrac{10^{-2}}{10^{-5}}=10^{3}$
$=1000$
The lower pH means the higher concentration, so P is $1000$ times greater.
